:::{#def-hessian}
#### Hessian matrix

Let $f$ be a scalar-valued function of a $p \times 1$ vector $\vx$
whose first partial derivatives exist on an open ball around $\vx$
and whose second partial derivatives exist at $\vx$.
The **Hessian matrix** of $f$ at $\vx$ is the derivative (@def-vector-valued-derivative)
of the gradient $\deriv{\vx} f(\vx)$ (@def-vector-derivative):

$$
\underbrace{\matr{H}_f(\vx)}_{p \times p} \eqdef \deriv{\vx} \tp{\paren{\deriv{\vx} f(\vx)}}.
$$

By @def-vector-valued-derivative, with $y_j = \deriv{x_j} f(\vx)$, its $(i, j)$ entry is

$$
\sb{\matr{H}_f(\vx)}_{ij} = \deriv{x_i} \paren{\deriv{x_j} f(\vx)}.
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-hessian}
#### A Hessian matrix

Let $f(\vx) = e^{2x_1 + x_2} - x_1$ for $\vx = \tp{(x_1, x_2)}$,
where $e$ is [Euler's number](algebra.qmd#def-euler-number),
and write $u = 2x_1 + x_2$.
By the [chain rule](calculus.qmd#thm-chain-rule),
$\deriv{x_1} e^{u} = 2 e^{u}$ and $\deriv{x_2} e^{u} = e^{u}$, so

$$
\deriv{\vx} f(\vx) = \sbmat{ 2 e^{u} - 1 \\ e^{u} }.
$$

Differentiating each entry again,

$$
\matr{H}_f(\vx)
= \sbmat{
\deriv{x_1} (2 e^{u} - 1) & \deriv{x_1} e^{u} \\
\deriv{x_2} (2 e^{u} - 1) & \deriv{x_2} e^{u}
}
= \sbmat{
4 e^{u} & 2 e^{u} \\
2 e^{u} & e^{u}
},
$$

and at $\vx = \vzero$, where $u = 0$,
$\matr{H}_f(\vzero) = \sbmat{ 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 }$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-hessian-missing}
#### A function with a gradient but no Hessian at a point

Let $f(\vx) = x_1 \abs{x_1}$ for $\vx = \tp{(x_1, x_2)}$,
where $\abs{\cdot}$ is the [absolute value](algebra.qmd#def-absolute-value).
For $x_1 > 0$, $f = x_1^2$ and $\deriv{x_1} f = 2 x_1$;
for $x_1 < 0$, $f = -x_1^2$ and $\deriv{x_1} f = -2 x_1$;
and at $x_1 = 0$ the difference quotient is $h \abs{h} / h = \abs{h} \to 0$.
So the gradient exists everywhere: it is $\tp{(2 \abs{x_1},\ 0)}$.
But $2 \abs{x_1}$ has no derivative in $x_1$ at $x_1 = 0$
(its difference quotient $2 \abs{h} / h$ is $2$ for $h > 0$ and $-2$ for $h < 0$),
so $\sb{\matr{H}_f(\vx)}_{11}$, and with it the Hessian, does not exist at any $\vx$ with $x_1 = 0$.

:::
